verdict: Everest's revenue fell 14% to $3.7B as it deliberately wrote less reinsurance, and $322M of catastrophe losses plus $268M of reserve strengthening held profit to $233M even as investment income rose 17% to $634M.

kpis.label: Revenue growth
kpis.note: Total revenues were $3,713M, vs $4,319M a year ago — premiums earned fell 18% by design

kpis.label: EPS (GAAP diluted)
kpis.note: Vs $6.09 a year ago; net operating EPS was $7.62

kpis.label: Combined ratio
kpis.note: Claims and underwriting costs per $100 of premiums — above 100% means underwriting lost money; it includes 10.5 points of catastrophe losses and 8.5 points of reserve strengthening

kpis.label: Net investment income
kpis.note: Up 17% YoY, on higher alternative-investment returns

segments.name: Reinsurance premiums earned
segments.note: Premiums from insuring other insurers (the Reinsurance Treaty segment) — Everest is deliberately writing less of this business, so earned premiums fell 13%.

segments.name: Insurance premiums earned
segments.note: Premiums from insuring businesses directly: Global Wholesale & Specialty contributed $705M (down 4%) and the run-off Legacy segment $208M (down 61% as that book shrinks).

segments.name: Net investment income & other
segments.note: Income from investing the premium float (money held before claims are paid): $634M of net investment income, minus $68M of net investment losses and $9M of other expense — clearly labeled here because it is not premium revenue.

opex.name: Commission, brokerage, taxes & fees
opex.note: Commissions and brokerage paid to win and place the business — about $24 per $100 of premiums earned.

opex.name: Other underwriting expenses
opex.note: The cost of running the underwriting operation.

opex.name: Corporate expenses
opex.note: Head-office costs not tied to a segment.

otherDetail: Other was -$36M: interest, fees and bond-issue cost amortization on Everest's debt.
oneTimers: Catastrophe losses were $322M before tax (10.5 points of the combined ratio), versus just $50M a year ago — storm and disaster claims are the swing factor in any insurer's quarter.

Everest strengthened prior-year casualty reinsurance reserves by about $268M before tax (8.5 points of the combined ratio) — an admission that claims from earlier years will cost more than first estimated. Group underwriting lost $223M before tax as a result.
footerNote: Insurer adaptation: premiums earned play the role of product revenue and claims (losses and loss adjustment expenses) play the role of cost of revenue. Claims are shown as $2,431M — $1M below the reported $2,432M — so the rounded $M lines reconcile exactly to the reported $233M net income; the release itself notes some amounts may not reconcile due to rounding. Segment premiums are net premiums earned by reportable segment from the release.

takeaways.title: Shrinking on purpose
takeaways.text: Net premiums earned fell 18% to $3,156M and total revenue fell 14% to $3,713M. Everest is walking away from reinsurance business it does not like the price of — gross written premiums in its core businesses fell 4%, with Reinsurance Treaty down 6% on a comparable basis while Global Wholesale & Specialty grew 3%.

takeaways.title: Claims overwhelmed underwriting
takeaways.text: The combined ratio hit 107.1% — $107 of claims and underwriting costs per $100 of premiums. Catastrophes cost $322M and prior-year reserve strengthening $268M; without those two items the attritional combined ratio was 88.4%. Reinsurance Treaty lost $191M before tax; Wholesale & Specialty still made $19M.

takeaways.title: Investments carried the quarter
takeaways.text: Net investment income rose 17% to $634M on stronger alternative-investment returns, which is most of why Everest still earned $233M ($6.12 per share) despite the underwriting loss. It also bought back $474M of its own shares in the quarter.

follow100Note: Rows are rounded to the nearest cent per $100; the chain adds to $6.27 of profit per $100 versus the $6.28 shown, a 1-cent rounding difference.
